what: A WebRTC SFU (selective forwarding unit) is a media server that receives each participant's audio or video track once and forwards it, unchanged, to whoever subscribes. LiveKit is an open-source SFU; voice AI agents join its rooms as ordinary participants.
like: Like a post-room sorter: every letter comes in once, and the sorter copies it into the right pigeonholes without opening or rewriting it.
why: Each person uploads one copy of their media, however many listen
The server never decodes media, so it stays cheap and adds little delay
An AI agent becomes just another participant: it hears the learner and talks back in the same room

steps.d: The learner's browser and the voice agent both join the same room with a short-lived token. Each is a participant with an identity.
The learner publishes one microphone track. The SFU forwards those packets to every subscriber without decoding or re-encoding them.
The agent subscribes to the learner's audio, runs speech-to-text, the model and text-to-speech, then publishes its own audio track back into the room.
The server and SDKs measure each subscriber's downstream bandwidth and adjust resolution or bitrate automatically.
Taps, option picks and canvas events travel on the data channel next to the audio, so voice and UI stay in one session.
One node needs nothing else; many nodes share Redis so every client in a room lands on the same node.

choices.d: Peer-to-peer for 2-3 people, an MCU when every viewer must get one mixed stream, an SFU when you want per-track control and cheap scaling - the usual choice for AI agents.
LiveKit Cloud runs the SFU, TURN and agent hosting for you; self-hosting gives control but you operate Redis, TURN and upgrades.
Close to the SFU region: every extra network hop adds to the voice latency budget.
Mint short-lived, room-scoped tokens on your server; the API key never reaches the browser.

instead.why: Fine for text and events, but raw audio over WebSockets lacks jitter buffers, echo cancellation and NAT traversal
For recorded media you upload and transcode, not live two-way audio

breaks.d: The agent runs in another region from the SFU.
breaks.see: Every turn is slower by a round trip; p95 latency drifts up
breaks.fix: Deploy agents in the SFU's region

breaks.d: WebRTC can't reach the server on UDP.
breaks.see: Some learners can't connect or audio drops
breaks.fix: TURN over TLS on port 443 as a fallback

breaks.d: The tutor's own voice comes back through the learner's speakers into the mic.
breaks.fix: Browser echo cancellation on, headphones hint, noise suppression

say: I put a WebRTC SFU between the learner and the agent - LiveKit - so audio is forwarded once with jitter buffers, echo cancellation and NAT traversal handled.
The agent joins the room as a participant and runs in the same region, so the network part of the latency budget stays small.
App events like taps and canvas updates ride the data channel in the same session.

followups.q: Why not stream audio over a WebSocket?
followups.a: It works for demos, but you lose WebRTC's jitter buffer, packet-loss concealment, echo cancellation and NAT traversal, which matter on real networks.
Each room lives on one node; more rooms means more nodes sharing Redis for routing. Agents are separate stateless workers dispatched per room.

today: Voice-agent frameworks such as LiveKit Agents treat the AI as a room participant, and LiveKit ships Agents UI components (control bar, audio visualizers, live transcript) installed through a shadcn registry.

check.q: What does an SFU do with a participant's audio?
check.a: Forwards it unchanged to each subscriber
d: Stores it and plays it later
check.why: An SFU routes packets without decoding them; mixing is what an MCU does.

check.q: How does an AI voice agent usually connect to a LiveKit room?
d: Through a webhook after the call
check.why: Agents subscribe to the learner's track and publish their own audio like any participant.

check.q: Learners behind strict firewalls can't connect. First fix?
check.a: TURN relay over TLS on port 443
check.why: TURN relays media when direct UDP is blocked.
